title: Dyslexia Early Intervention: The Mom Who Built a School for Her Daughter
guestBio: Cathy Johnson is a licensed Speech-Language Pathologist and the founder of The Johnson Academy — the only school for children with dyslexia in South Orange County — and the Speech, Language and Learning Center in San Juan Capistrano. After her own daughter was diagnosed with dyslexia in kindergarten, Cathy built a school, developed an Orton-Gillingham teacher-training program at the University of La Verne, and launched the nonprofit Ready to Read to fund scholarships for families who need them. She has spent more than 20 years consulting for school districts and fighting for the third-grade window every child deserves.
excerpt: Speech-language pathologist Cathy Johnson built a school after her own daughter's dyslexia diagnosis — and what she learned will change how you advocate for your child. From the third-grade window to why "let's wait" is never a plan, this episode is for every mom who knows something is wrong.

quiz.title: What Kind of Advocate Are You For Your Child?
quiz.description: Every mother navigates her child's struggles differently — shaped by her instincts, her history, her bandwidth, and how she was taught to trust (or not trust) the systems around her. This quiz isn't about right or wrong answers. It's about understanding your natural advocacy style so you can show up even more powerfully for the child who needs you.

A.name: The Gut-First Advocate
A.description: You have always led with instinct, and when something feels off with your child, you feel it in your whole body before you have a single data point to back it up. You don't need a specialist to tell you what you already know — but you sometimes struggle to translate that knowing into action inside systems that demand paperwork and patience. Your superpower is that you won't let anyone gaslight you out of what you see. This episode will validate everything your gut has been telling you and give you the language to make the system listen.

B.name: The Research-Led Mom
B.description: Before you make a move, you read everything — the studies, the forums, the parent Facebook groups, the clinical guidelines. You feel most confident when your instincts are backed by evidence, and you show up to appointments with notes. The challenge is that information overload can sometimes delay action, because there is always one more thing to learn before you feel ready. This episode will hand you exactly the research you need and give you permission to stop gathering and start moving.

C.name: The Trust-the-System Mom
C.description: You were raised to believe that teachers and doctors know best, and part of you still holds onto that — even when something doesn't feel right. You bring your concerns to the professionals in your child's life and try hard to trust their guidance, even when the guidance is "let's wait." Your grace and your willingness to collaborate are genuine strengths. This episode will help you understand what the system gets wrong about dyslexia and why advocating harder is not the same as being difficult.

D.name: The Builder Mom
D.description: When the solution your child needs doesn't exist, your mind immediately goes to: then I'll create it. You are entrepreneurial by nature, you don't wait for permission, and you have a high tolerance for the discomfort of building something from nothing. Cathy Johnson is your people. This episode will speak directly to the part of you that knows the problem in front of you might be pointing at your purpose — and give you the courage to take the first step.

content:
There is a moment that every mother of a struggling reader knows. You are sitting at the kitchen table watching your child stare at a page, and you can feel the effort radiating off of them — the concentration, the frustration, the slow erosion of confidence that no homework chart or extra reading night seems to touch. You bring it up at the parent-teacher conference and someone says, "Let's give it time. Some kids just develop at their own pace." And you smile and nod, but your gut says something completely different.

This episode is for that moment. And for every moment after it.

Aimee's oldest son was diagnosed with dyslexia in first grade. After his very first day at The Johnson Academy, he came home and said, "Mom, no one ever taught me how to read before." One day. That sentence — from a child who had been in school, sitting in classrooms, doing the work — is the gut-punch that opens this conversation and sets the tone for everything Cathy Johnson shares across the next hour.

When the Problem in Front of You Is Pointing at Your Purpose

Cathy Johnson did not set out to build a school. She was a licensed Speech-Language Pathologist with a clinical practice, a professional, a mom — and then her daughter was diagnosed with dyslexia in kindergarten. The school said the right things. The years passed. And then one morning in fifth grade, her daughter woke up and said she was not going to school anymore. Not as a tantrum. As a decision.

Cathy did not fight the district. She did not wait for the next IEP meeting. She built a school. That was twenty years ago. The Johnson Academy is now the only school for children with dyslexia in South Orange County, and what started as a mother's refusal to accept the system has grown into a teacher-training program at the University of La Verne, a nonprofit called Ready to Read that funds scholarships, and consulting work with school districts across the region.

The throughline Cathy names clearly: sometimes the problem in front of you is pointing directly at your purpose. Her daughter's struggle did not derail her career. It became her life's work.

The Third-Grade Window — and Why "Let's Watch Her" Has a Cost

One of the most important and urgent things Cathy shares in this episode is what the research actually says about timing. The brain's window for foundational literacy acquisition is widest before third grade. That does not mean intervention after third grade is useless — Cathy is emphatic on this point, and she has the stories to back it up, including teaching a 70-year-old to read. But it does mean that every semester spent in a "watch and wait" posture has a measurable cost.

If your child has a speech delay at age five, that is a clinical warning sign for dyslexia — not a phase, not a personality quirk, not something to monitor loosely. It should trigger a screening conversation with a qualified specialist. Screening can happen at age four, before a child has even seen a letter, and identifying risk that early changes the entire trajectory of what intervention looks like.

Cathy is precise about what "intervention" actually means, because it is not what most schools offer. Accommodations are not intervention. Giving a child extended time on a test, or letting them listen to an audiobook, does not teach them to decode. It helps them function inside a system that was not built for their brain — and that has value — but it is not the same as actually teaching the child to read.

Teach the Way the Brain Learns

What does real instruction look like for a child with dyslexia? Cathy walks through the principles of multisensory, structured literacy — the approach underpinning methodologies like Orton-Gillingham and Wilson Reading — in a way that is completely accessible even if you have never heard those terms before.

The core insight is this: a dyslexic brain needs to receive information through multiple pathways simultaneously in order for it to "file" correctly into long-term memory. When Cathy describes a child writing a letter in the air with their whole arm while saying the sound out loud, she is not describing a novelty activity — she is describing the mechanism by which a sound finally sticks. Hearing it alone does not work for this brain. Seeing it alone does not work. But hearing it, saying it, feeling it, and moving it together? That works.

This is also why more reading practice — the instinctive parental and school response to a child who struggles to read — can actively make things worse. You are not building a stronger pathway. You are reinforcing the wrong pattern, over and over, faster and faster. The answer is never more of what is not working. The answer is a fundamentally different method.

What to Look for When You're Hiring Help

Cathy is refreshingly direct about the tutor and program landscape. A weekend certificate in Orton-Gillingham does not qualify someone to intervene with a dyslexic child. What you are looking for is year-long, supervised training in a structured methodology, with ongoing mentorship and practicum hours. That bar exists for a reason, and it matters enormously for your child's outcome. Cathy also shares what a one-minute-a-day phonemic awareness activity looks like — something any parent can start doing at home tonight — because early exposure and practice at the sound level, before letters ever enter the picture, is foundational.

The Mom Who Refuses to Wait Is Not Being Difficult

If there is one permission this episode gives every mother listening, it is this: your instinct is data. You are not being anxious. You are not projecting. When your child is working harder than every other child in the class and still falling further behind, and the school is asking you to wait, you are allowed to stop waiting. You are allowed to ask harder questions, seek a private evaluation, and demand instruction — not accommodation.

Cathy built The Johnson Academy because she refused to wait. Aimee's son said "no one ever taught me how to read before" because someone finally did. Your child's story is not written yet. And as Cathy says with full clinical confidence: there really is no such thing as too late — but earlier is always better, and before third grade is the window worth fighting for.

If this episode moved you, share it with the mother in your life who is sitting at that kitchen table right now. She needs to hear this.
